context: Round 4 builds Squire's signed updates with rollback, and its support tickets with a preview, an outbox and retries, from nothing: at the round's base there is no update code, no release format, no version, no release key, no ticket code and no install id, and lay-down keeps one copy of core, so there is nothing to roll back to. Three facts shape it. Re-running the app after an update would lay an older core down unchecked, because set-up lays the app's core down whenever it differs from the release folder. Every yes and every "shown" passes through Squire's own session: the floor refuses any core change from inside the session, yes or no, so installs, rollbacks and sends are made by the scheduler's tick after a recorded yes, as round 3's known fixes are, and the owner sees a request only as the session relays the floor's block. And Claude Code updates itself outside Squire. Runtime facts below come from the documentation named (code.claude.com setup: the launcher, its versions folder, background updates, autoUpdatesChannel and minimumVersion; man ssh-keygen and man sshd on macOS 26.3.1 for -Y sign, -Y verify and the allowed-signers format; man launchd.plist for KeepAlive and ThrottleInterval), from ADR-003 and ADR-004, or from the probes on a test Mac (each marked measured, with its evidence file). Anything no source states outright is marked inferred.
decision:
1. The first design fact: re-running the app after an update never lays an older core down unchecked. Set-up's layDown end state holds when the Squire home's current kept release is the app's own core (as in round 3), or is a release installed by a verified update whose version is at or above the app's version. An app older than the installed release is refused one thing only, laying its core down: the step's end state holds over the newer release, and nothing of core, the kept releases or the agents changes. The rest of the re-run proceeds as in round 3 (the sign-in repair ADR-004 names among it, so opening the installer to sign in again still works), and the run tells the owner on "Squire: set-up paused" that the Squire already installed is newer than the app it ran from, so its core was not laid down (no window is added). An app newer than the installed release (a fresh download) lays down as in round 3; its signature check is the public release's first-install check, not this round's. The floor fix (ADR-004 line 17) lays down the current kept release, never the app's core. The app's version is the version in its core's release.json (line 4).
2. What a release is. A release is core/ plus manifest.json plus manifest.json.sig. manifest.json is one JSON object with exactly four fields: version (the release's version, line 3), files (every file under core/, by its path relative to core/, to its SHA-256 as 64 lower-case hex digits), changelog (the plain-words text of what the release changes, for the owner) and claudeCodeTested (the lowest Claude Code version the release was tested with). manifest.json.sig is the signature of manifest.json's exact bytes made with ssh-keygen -Y sign and the namespace squire-release (man ssh-keygen). On the release host a release is one gzip tar file holding those three at its top and nothing else, and latest.json beside it, {"version": <the release's version>, "archive": <the tar file's name>}, names the newest release; latest.json is not signed and is only a pointer.
3. The version. Three whole numbers joined by dots (0.1.0), compared as numbers part by part, as ADR-004 line 6 compares macOS versions. Anything else in a version field is not a version, and a release carrying one is refused.
4. The trust root and the addresses. core/release-key.pub is the one public key an installed Squire trusts: a floor file under the digests lay-down records (ADR-003 line 6), laid down from the app's core at first install and afterwards only by a signed release. core/release.json is a floor file under the same digests holding the core's version, the release host's address (releaseHost, a base address ending in a slash, under which latest.json and each release archive are fetched) and the support intake's address (intake, where a ticket is posted). A release is checked only with the installed key, never with a key inside the incoming release. A release signed by the installed key may carry a new core/release-key.pub; once it is installed, that key checks the next release, so a key can move to new hardware without a reinstall. The check builds an allowed-signers file in the staging folder from the installed key with the identity squire-release and namespaces="squire-release" (man sshd, ALLOWED SIGNERS) and runs /usr/bin/ssh-keygen -Y verify -f <allowed signers> -I squire-release -n squire-release -s manifest.json.sig with manifest.json on its standard input, bounded at 30 seconds, in the environment ADR-004 line 3 builds (measured on a test Mac with OpenSSH_10.2p1 from an environment built from nothing: -Y sign exits 0, and -Y verify exits 0 for a good signature and 255 for a missing signature, another key, a manifest changed by one byte and another namespace; round-4 define-probes r1-ssh-keygen.txt). A test world lays a core whose release-key.pub is a test key made in its own temporary folder and whose release.json names its loopback stand-ins; no environment variable or other switch redirects updates or tickets. Before the public release a production check finds no latest.json and reads "could not check".
5. The check, fail closed. A release is staged, and so may be offered, only when all of these hold: ssh-keygen -Y verify exits 0 against the installed key; manifest.json parses as one object with exactly the four known fields, each of its type, and a version above the installed one; the archive holds only core/, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig, every entry a plain file or folder whose path stays inside it; every file the manifest lists is present under core/ with its digest; and no file under core/ is unlisted. Anything the check cannot run, read or parse is a refusal: no ssh-keygen, an ssh-keygen that fails or passes its bound, an archive that does not unpack, a field it does not know. Downloads and their unpacked files live in staging/ in the Squire home, outside core; a refused release's staging is removed, nothing of the installed core, the kept releases, the agents or the owner's folder changes, and the refusal is one health line, "update: Squire refused release <version>: <reason>; nothing was changed" (the version latest.json names), until the next weekly check.
6. Where releases live. The Squire home keeps releases/<version>/ (core/, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig as checked) for the current release and the previous one, and current-release.json, the current-release record {"current": <version>, "previous": <version or null>, "verified": true when the current release was installed by a verified update}, written whole through a file beside it and a rename. The previous release is removed only after the install's check passes, so at most two are kept, with a third briefly during an install. Round 3's release/core, the app's core set-up kept, becomes the first kept release at the first update: the install copies it, checked by digest, into releases/<its version>/core. Lay-down's guard names releases/ in the Squire home (and release/core, for set-up) instead of release/core alone.
7. The weekly check. The wake-ups scheduler's existing 60-second tick (wake-up.py --due; no new agent) runs the check when update.json in the Squire home records no check in the last 7 days (lastCheck, seconds since the epoch, recorded at every check whatever its outcome): it fetches latest.json from releaseHost, and when it names a version above the installed one, downloads the archive into staging/, checks it (line 5) and stages it: a verified release waits, as checked, in staging/<version>/ (core/, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig), and nothing else of a download is left in staging/. Every request is bounded at 30 seconds to connect and 30 seconds for each read, and a download at 10 minutes in all; a fetch that fails, times out, is cut short or does not parse is "could not check", recorded in update.json and the log, removes its staging and is tried at the next weekly check. A verified release staged sends one wake-up through Squire's own router naming the version and the request that asks for it, /usr/bin/python3 <Squire home>/core/tools/update.py --install <version>; a staged release waiting for a yes is mentioned again at most once a week. No update is offered, staged or installed while the health check names any fault, so a fault after an install is the install's: while it names one the weekly check does not run and records nothing, and it runs at the first tick after the fault is gone. A latest.json naming a version at or below the installed one downloads nothing and offers nothing. A verified release newer than one already staged replaces it (only the newest is staged), and a yes for the version it replaced is no yes. Within one tick the weekly check runs before any install. update.json records each check's time (lastCheck) and its outcome (staged, refused, nothing newer, or could not check).
8. The offer, and what "shown" means. The session asks for the install by running the request line; the safety floor never lets it run in the session, yes or no, and asks the owner for it: its block names the request and carries the version and the release's changelog exactly as the staged manifest holds them, then a blank line, then these words, verbatim: "Show the owner the text above inside a fenced code block: a line of three backticks with no language name, then the text exactly as written, unchanged, with nothing added inside the fence, then a line of three backticks. Your own words go only outside the fence. Then wait for their answer." "Shown" and "previewed" in the update and ticket criteria mean this: the exact text Squire's own code puts in the floor's block, which the session shows the owner as the body of one fenced code block (no language name), byte for byte, and which the bound tests compare with what is installed or posted. Measured on a test Mac (round-4 define-probes r2-relay.txt): told only to show the text exactly as written, the session relayed it word for word inside a Markdown blockquote, twice; with the words above it showed it inside one fence, equal byte for byte on the raw message (657 bytes, underscores and asterisks kept). A blockquote is not used: a Markdown renderer can eat underscores, asterisks and line breaks inside a ticket's JSON, and a fence renders its body as written. Lay-down's instructions for the session (the CLAUDE.md it writes) carry the same words. The pre-ruled fallback, a Mac dialog carrying the exact text with "Install" and "Later" (or "Send" and "Don't send"), is not taken.
9. The yes and its freshness, one rule for the known fixes, the update and the ticket. The owner's yes is the approvals ledger's answer record for that request (ADR-004 line 17), its time "at" in seconds since the epoch. The outside job acts on a yes only when it is exact (an update's yes names that version and that version is still the staged, verified one; a ticket's yes names that ticket and the outbox file's digest is unchanged; a fix's yes names a fault still present), fresh (given less than 30 minutes before the outside job reads it, and not after the moment it reads it) and unused; it marks the yes used under the ledger's lock before it acts. A yes timed after now is no yes: it changes nothing, the result says it could not try, and the session's request is asked again. A stale, mismatched or used yes changes nothing either. Until a fresh, exact yes, core's digests and the kept releases stay as they are.
10. The install and the check. The tick runs the install from the installed (previous) release's own code, /usr/bin/python3 -B <Squire home>/core/tools/update.py --perform, bounded, and the install is held to its end. Its named steps, in order (measured on a test Mac: a Remote Control session and its server stayed up through 7 lay-downs of a changed core, about 110 ms each, and 371 floor-hook calls, 96 of them during a lay-down, all answered as before, so the order stands; round-4 define-probes r3-live-lay-down.txt): record (install.json written in the Squire home before the first change, naming the two versions, the install process's id and start time, and the step reached (step), written again at each step, through a file beside it and a rename); keep (the new release copied into releases/<version>/ and checked by digest against its manifest, round 3's release/core kept as the previous release at the first update); stop (the agents booted out in the account's own home, then any runner still holding its lock and its server's process group ended, waiting at most 30 seconds for the lock to be free); lay (lay-down from releases/<version>/core); switch (current-release.json names the new release); reload (the agents loaded again in the account's own home); check; clear (install.json removed last). The check is ADR-004 lines 12 and 13's end states, read again: the runner holding its lock within 30 seconds, every floor file at its digest, signed in, no server stopped before a session, one live session within 2 minutes, plus every installed core file against the new release's signed manifest, and no process of the previous release still running. A check line it cannot read is a failure. A passing check removes the release before the previous one and sends one wake-up: "Squire is updated to <version>; all checks passed".
11. The rollback. On any failure of the check the install job, still the previous release's code, lays the previous release down again, switches current-release.json back, reloads, checks again, and sends one wake-up naming both versions: Squire rolled <new> back to <previous>. No one acts. If the second check fails too, a health line names both versions and offers a support ticket (line 15). A rolled-back release stays out of the offer until a newer one is published.
12. An install that does not finish. install.json is written before the install's first change and removed last, so at every runner start and every scheduler tick its presence means an install did not finish (a restart, a power cut, a killed process, a log-out), unless the install process it names is still running with that start time: that is an install in progress, and the runner starts as usual. Then: if the new release's files under releases/<version>/, the installed core's digests and the signed manifest all match and the check passes, Squire stays on the new release; otherwise it lays the previous release down, as a rollback. Either way one wake-up says which, "Squire's update did not finish; Squire is on <version>", and install.json is removed. A download that fails, times out or is cut short never reaches core (line 7). The owner's folder is never written by an install, a rollback or a recovery: the one record an update adds there is the approvals ledger's use of the owner's yes ({type: use, request, at}), written before the install starts.
13. What an update never touches. The owner's folder (~/Squire): every entry's relative path, type, permissions, bytes and link target are the same before an install, after it and after a rollback (times are not compared: a read changes them), whatever the entry (a file no one may read, a link to nothing or outside the folder, an empty or closed folder, a named pipe), except Squire's own records inside it (the approvals ledger and Squire's state files there), whose only permitted change across an update and a rollback is the one recorded use of the owner's yes (line 12). The install, the rollback and the recovery write only in the Squire home and, for the agents, Library/LaunchAgents. The name and personality stay in the owner's squire.json; lay-down writes them again into CLAUDE.md and the runner passes --name, so they are unchanged after an update and after a rollback (ADR-004 line 15). Round 3's gap in the floor digests over core/lib/squire.py between installs stays written; each install closes it, since every core file is checked against the signed manifest.
14. Claude Code changed outside Squire. At every start the runner records claude --version and the launcher's resolved target (~/.local/bin/claude followed to its file; setup page: the launcher is a link into ~/.local/share/claude/versions/) in claude-code.json in the Squire home. The scheduler's tick compares both with what the runner recorded, each minute: any difference, or a value it cannot read (claude --version exiting non-zero, printing something else or not answering within 30 seconds; a launcher that points at nothing), runs the health check and sends its result in one wake-up, "Claude Code changed outside Squire (<what changed>); the health check says: <its lines, or all checks passed>", with the known fixes it offers (reload Squire's agents, sign in again); the same values are not reported twice. No Claude Code downgrade is ever offered: Squire does not manage Claude Code's versions folder (setup page: it keeps the two newest versions and deletes the rest). The update keys autoUpdatesChannel and minimumVersion live in core's settings, laid down and guarded by ADR-003 line 6's equality, as the builder's hygiene with no criterion. Measured on a test Mac from the runner's environment: claude --version prints "<x.y.z> (Claude Code)" and exits 0, and the launcher is a link to ~/.local/share/claude/versions/<version>, a plain file owned by the user (round-4 define-probes r4-claude-version.txt).
15. Which results offer a ticket. A known fix's result "fixed: <fault>" offers no ticket; "still: <fault>" offers one; "could not try: <fault>: <reason>" offers none and asks for the fix again. A fault not on the known-fixes list (ADR-004 line 17: an ignored overlay, a server that stopped before any session, a backup that could not run) offers a ticket; a moved settings file stays named only. A second check that fails after a rollback offers one (line 11). The result of the last known fix is kept in fixes.json, and printed by every run of the health check, by the session or by the owner, until the owner answers the request of the ticket it offered or the fix is asked for again; a read never consumes it. A ticket offer is its own health line, "ticket: <ticket id> is ready to send about <fault>; to send it, ask: /usr/bin/python3 <Squire home>/core/tools/ticket.py --send <ticket id>", and never sits on a fault's own line.
16. The ticket. A ticket is built once, by the health check run (whoever runs it) or the outside job that first offers it, and kept while it waits: outbox/<ticket id>.json in the Squire home holds its bytes, and outbox/<ticket id>.state.json its record, {"digest": <the bytes' SHA-256, 64 lower-case hex digits>, "request": <the request id the owner answered, or null>, "attempts": [{"at": <seconds since the epoch>, "outcome"}]}; a fault already offered names the same ticket at every later run while it waits; once it is sent or set aside, the fault's next occurrence builds a new ticket. It is one JSON object whose fields come only from this allow-list, each value from a closed set or a fixed pattern: ticketId (t- and 32 lower-case hex digits), installId (line 17), destination (the intake's address from core's release.json), squireVersion and claudeCodeVersion (versions), macOSVersion (whole numbers and dots), macModelClass (from sysctl hw.model: MacBookAir... is MacBook Air, MacBookPro... MacBook Pro, Macmini... Mac mini, iMac... iMac, MacPro... Mac Pro, and Mac<n>,<n> is Mac; any other answer drops the field), agentsLoaded (the three agent labels lay-down writes), healthCodes (the health check's result codes, each a lower-case word or words joined by hyphens), lastErrors (each {"code", "at"}: a code of lower-case words joined by hyphens and a time in seconds since the epoch), fixesTried (the known fixes' names: runner, floor, sign-in) and createdAt (seconds since the epoch). There is no free text, no raw message, no file name, no path, no computer name and no account name, and no sentence from the owner in this version. A value outside its field's set or pattern drops that field. The privacy patterns (email addresses, phone numbers, card numbers, and the account's own short and full names) run over the result as a second net, and a hit drops the field.
17. The preview, the yes and the send. The session asks to send by running the request line of line 14; the floor never lets it run in the session and asks the owner for it: its block is the request, then the outbox file's exact bytes, install id and destination included, then the words to show the owner that text exactly as written. The yes names that request, and approves the bytes its block showed: the floor records the outbox file's digest with the request. The outside job (the scheduler's tick, /usr/bin/python3 -B <Squire home>/core/tools/ticket.py --perform) posts that file's bytes and nothing else to the intake, after checking the file's digest, as one HTTP POST with Content-Type application/json, bounded at 30 seconds to connect and 30 seconds for the answer. A no, or no answer within the ledger's timeout, posts nothing and sets the ticket aside (outbox/set-aside/). A yes naming another request posts nothing.
18. The install id. 128 random bits from the operating system's random source, written as 32 lower-case hex digits, made at the first ticket and kept in install-id in the Squire home (0600); the same on every ticket from one Squire home, made from nothing about the owner, the Mac or the account, and registered nowhere: enrolment in this version is this id alone. What the receiver keeps, and deletion at the owner's request, are the live receiver's, a later round's.
19. Kept and retried. An approved ticket whose send fails, finds the intake offline or gets no answer within the bound stays in the outbox, and a health line says it is waiting to send, "ticket: <ticket id> is waiting to send (<n> attempts so far)". The scheduler's tick retries it with a growing wait, read from the attempts in its record: 1 minute after the first attempt, then 2, 4, 8 and so on, doubling up to a ceiling of 6 hours between attempts, for as long as it waits. Every attempt sends the same bytes with the same ticketId; the intake treats a ticketId it already holds as already filed. The digest is checked before every attempt against the digest the yes approved, and a file changed after the yes is never sent; it waits for another yes to a request whose block showed the changed bytes. An answer in the 2xx range clears it from the outbox.
20. Accepted residuals, written at this round's open. Residuals (a) to (c) of ADR-004 stay accepted in writing for the release, and (d) stays accepted. Round 3's floor items (the Keychain command class's code, a lock on the wake-up router, a claude in a folder others can write, a job with no record, an unreadable record) each stay a written residual until the round that opens the floor again. The floor digests' gap over core/lib/squire.py between installs stays written, and each install closes it (line 13). A forged ledger stays an accepted residual, with no test. Retiring a leaked release key is the public release's question: a holder of the key could sign a rotation too.
consequences:
Usage model for every budget and cap the update and ticket criteria carry; every figure is an assumption unless a source is named.
The weekly check. Typical: one small latest.json fetch a week (under 1 KB), and a release archive of core (about 200 KB to 1 MB of text and scripts) a few times a year; a check takes seconds. Heavy: a slow or captive network makes each request wait its 30-second bounds and the archive its 10-minute bound once, then "could not check" until next week; nothing breaks and nothing is retried that week.
The 60-second tick. Typical: a tick with nothing pending costs one ledger read, one look at update.json, install.json and the outbox, and the Claude Code comparison (claude --version, bounded at 30 seconds, and one link read). Heavy: an install or a rollback holds that tick for up to about 3 minutes (the lock wait, lay-down, the 30-second runner wait and the 2-minute session wait, twice on a rollback); the scheduler's next run does not start while one runs (launchd does not start a job again while it is running, man launchd.plist).
The ledger's timeout and the yes's freshness. A request is open for the ledger's timeout (approvalTimeoutSeconds, 600 by default) and a yes is acted on within 30 minutes. Typical: the owner answers within a minute and the tick acts within the next minute. Heavy: the owner answers after the request closed: nothing happens and the session asks again.
Downloads. 30 seconds to connect and for each read, 10 minutes in all. Typical: seconds. Heavy: a 1 MB archive at 2 KB a second takes under 10 minutes and never sits 30 seconds without a byte.
The ticket retry. 1, 2, 4, 8 minutes and onwards, doubling to a ceiling of 6 hours between attempts. Typical: the intake answers the first post, or the Mac is offline for an hour and the ticket goes within minutes of reconnecting. Heavy: no intake before the live receiver exists, so an approved ticket waits, tried about four times a day at the ceiling, each attempt one small POST.
The 2-minute session wait in the check, ADR-004 line 12's. Typical: seconds (round 2's walk: the record 5 seconds after lay-down). Heavy: a slow first start after an update; past 2 minutes the check fails and the release is rolled back.
Disk for two kept releases. Typical: two copies of core, about 0.5 to 2 MB, and a third during an install. Heavy: a release that grows core tenfold still costs tens of MB; staging is removed after every check.
Measured on a test Mac (round-4 define-probes, results.json), every fact the probes were to settle: the ssh-keygen command line and its exits from an environment built from nothing (line 4, r1-ssh-keygen.txt); the session's relay of a floor block, word for word inside a blockquote when told to show it exactly as written and byte for byte inside one fenced code block with line 8's words (r2-relay.txt); a lay-down under a running runner, which left the live session, its server and every hook call part way through the copy as they were, so the order of stop and lay stands (line 10, r3-live-lay-down.txt); the form of claude --version and the launcher's target, and the connected line showing the session folder's name, not --name (line 14, r4-claude-version.txt).
Inferred: that macOS 13's ssh-keygen has -Y sign and -Y verify (OpenSSH 8.1 and later have them; macOS 13's own is a release Verify line); that the owner's own Claude Code and Squire's share the one launcher, so either can move it; that access times change on a read, which is why the owner's-folder hash leaves times out.
For the release Verify, by hand, never a round test: a real restart part way through an update, a real release fetched from the public repository with no account, the real key's signature on the release candidate, and macOS 13's ssh-keygen.

alternativesConsidered.name: A core/current link switched in one change
alternativesConsidered.summary: The discovery's shape: unpack beside, then switch a link.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Lay-down already copies core whole and swaps it with a rename; a link adds a second mechanism for the same switch, and the kept releases already give rollback its source.

alternativesConsidered.name: One slot, and a fresh download to roll back
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A rollback would need the network and the release host at the moment an update has just failed; two kept releases cost a few MB.

alternativesConsidered.name: Three instances of a bad release only
alternativesConsidered.summary: Refuse a missing signature, another key and an altered manifest.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A signature over the manifest alone passes a file added to the bundle and a listed file that is missing; the check decides the class (exactly the files the key signed) and refuses what it cannot read.

alternativesConsidered.name: A weekly launchd agent of its own
alternativesConsidered.summary: A fourth agent for the update check.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The scheduler's 60-second tick already performs recorded requests; a recorded last-check time makes the check weekly with no new agent.

alternativesConsidered.name: A Mac dialog for the changelog and the ticket preview from the start
alternativesConsidered.summary: Show the exact text in a dialog.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: The owner may be on the phone, and a dialog is a box on the screen; it stays the pre-ruled fallback if the session does not relay a block verbatim.

alternativesConsidered.name: The session's relay, unmeasured
alternativesConsidered.summary: Take the session's words as the preview.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A privacy promise cannot rest on a model's words alone; the tests assert the block's text and a probe measures the relay.

alternativesConsidered.name: The health check rolls back on a later tick
alternativesConsidered.summary: Roll back when the next check notices.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: "With no one acting" needs the check and the rollback in the same outside job as the install, run from the previous release's code.

alternativesConsidered.name: One kill point for an interrupted install
alternativesConsidered.summary: Prove recovery after one chosen interruption.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: An install can stop at any step; the install record and its named steps make recovery decide the class, and the tests kill it at every step.

alternativesConsidered.name: Watch Claude Code only at the runner's start
alternativesConsidered.summary: Compare versions when the runner starts.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Claude Code updates in the background and takes effect at its next start, which may be days away; the tick compares every minute.

alternativesConsidered.name: Privacy patterns only for the ticket
alternativesConsidered.summary: Copy diagnostics and scrub them with patterns.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A name cannot be found by a pattern; only fields built from closed sets and fixed patterns keep personal details out, with the patterns as a second net.

alternativesConsidered.name: Enrolment at a server
alternativesConsidered.summary: Register each install with the intake.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Before the live receiver exists there is nothing to register with; a random install id kept on the Mac is enough for this version and registers nothing.

alternativesConsidered.name: Send a ticket once and report
alternativesConsidered.summary: No retry after the owner's yes.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: An approved ticket would be lost to a dropped connection; keeping it in the outbox with the same id, and the digest checked before each attempt, keeps it exactly as approved.

alternativesConsidered.name: Addresses from an environment variable
alternativesConsidered.summary: Point updates and tickets at a test server through the environment.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A program already running as the owner could redirect them; the addresses live in a core file under the floor's digests, and the test world lays a core naming its loopback stand-ins.

alternativesConsidered.name: An app that refuses to run at all after an update
alternativesConsidered.summary: Block the installer once an update is installed.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: Opening the installer again is the way to sign in again after a sign-in ends; it must still run its earlier steps, laying nothing older down.

alternativesConsidered.name: A Markdown blockquote for the relay
alternativesConsidered.summary: Let the session show a block as a quotation, as it did when told only to show it exactly as written.
alternativesConsidered.reasonNotChosen: A quotation renders as Markdown: underscores, asterisks and line breaks inside a ticket's JSON can be eaten, so what the owner sees may not be what is sent; a fenced code block shows its body as written, and the relay probe measured it byte for byte.

title: Signed updates kept two deep with rollback and recovery, the Claude Code watch, and support tickets built once into an outbox, previewed through the floor and retried exactly as approved
